selected_news.title: Claude, Riemann Hipotezini Çözdü: İki Grup Doğruladı
selected_news.summary: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out. Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
selected_news.article_text: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis A mathematician at Anthropic has convincingly said that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems “Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.” The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859 The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is” He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”

selected_news.title: COP31’de Fosil Yakıt Terimi Taslaktan Silindi
selected_news.summary: UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
selected_news.source_headline: UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned
selected_news.article_text: UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year's U.N. climate summit reaches its final day ANTALYA, Turkey -- This year's U.N. climate talks are wrapping up in Turkey, with negotiators still debating how to address global warming and experts warning that only slashing fossil fuels can avert its most catastrophic effects. Activists and country leaders were in an uproar Friday, the last scheduled day of the two-week summit known as COP31, after the term “fossil fuels” was left out of the final agreement’s draft. Climate summits often end with a final text, meant to address how the world will deal with climate change. Such agreements — often adopted by nearly 200 nations — are still voluntary and non-binding. Negotiators, who pulled an all-nighter from Thursday into Friday, said they expect COP31 to go into overtime on Saturday. Past COPs have failed to agree on how to transition away from fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — that warm the planet, heat the oceans and worsen air quality. Climate change also intensified several of this year's disasters, like Europe’s deadly heat waves and Nepal’s devastating flooding. If phasing out fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement, this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. In a rare move, Panama vowed to “formally object” if the final agreement doesn’t add climate finance, cap oil production, and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country's Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed. “The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility,” he said. “What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air.” In the lead up to COP31, the United Nations announced the world is dangerously close to missing its decades-old goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. “There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South,” said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read “SHAME!” One of the main deals on the table at COP31 is an electrification goal to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035. But the final draft doesn't spell out that this should be reached with renewable energy sources, like solar and wind — leaving the door open for fossil fuel power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push. “At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress,” said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa. The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years but it was only in 2021 during COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, that nations first acknowledged fossil fuels contribute to climate change. Two years later during COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time. Turkey and Australia, co-hosts of COP31, are being roundly criticized for removing fossil fuels from the final text's draft. “We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs,” said Turkey's Minister of Environment Murat Kurum, who is overseeing the summit held in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. The electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, he said. “Removing those words from a document will not remove the pollution from the atmosphere," said Adow of Power Shift Africa. “It simply exposes how far these negotiations have become detached from what is needed outside this conference center.” Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable nations that don't emit a lot of greenhouse gases — have said that rich countries are not providing previously agreed upon funds to deal with climate change. They said that U.N. funds for adapting to climate risks, dealing with climate impacts and funds for clean energy infrastructure don’t match what the U.N. has said these countries need. The draft agreement states the need to triple the amount of money for countries adapting to climate impacts, but it doesn’t specify how much. One of the draft's previous versions stated at least $120 billion would be needed annually. Many of the world's most polluting nations did not participate directly at this year's talks, including the United States, the world’s largest economy and a major emitter. It's richer nations, like the U.S., that vulnerable countries want funding from — and it's hard to ask for funds without American officials in the room. Efforts to slow global warming have essentially stalled for the past five years, according to a recent report by the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker. “Disappointment is rife," said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, an adviser to African negotiators in Turkey. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027. “Hope is not lost, but absent a course correction, we are headed toward a low-ambition set of outcomes at COP31,” he said. ___ Delgado reported from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press writer Tammy Webber contributed to this report from Fenton, Michigan. ___ The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. selected_news.title: Queensland’da 7 ölüm ve bir intihar: Sağlık krizi
selected_news.summary: A government in office for more than two years is finally forced to take responsibility and seemingly no longer able to blame its Labor predecessors Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast At the beginning of another Queensland parliamentary sitting week, anonymous sources were out in force, this time background briefing against the state’s Labor leader, Steven Miles. It is no great revelation to observers of Queensland politics that Miles, still seemingly bruised from his election loss two years ago, has struggled to find his feet as opposition leader. Many wondered why he wanted to stay on after the party’s drubbing in 2024. Some of Labor’s factional whisperers were telling anyone who would listen that the former premier’s leadership would come to an end in the weeks before Christmas. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: ‘Six, seven, maybe more preventable deaths’: Queensland’s LNP faces reckoning over broken health system
selected_news.article_text: A government in office for more than two years is finally forced to take responsibility and seemingly no longer able to blame its Labor predecessors Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast At the beginning of another Queensland parliamentary sitting week, anonymous sources were out in force, this time background briefing against the state’s Labor leader, Steven Miles It is no great revelation to observers of Queensland politics that Miles, still seemingly bruised from his election loss two years ago, has struggled to find his feet as opposition leader. Many wondered why he wanted to stay on after the party’s drubbing in 2024. Some of Labor’s factional whisperers were telling anyone who would listen that the former premier’s leadership would come to an end in the weeks before Christmas However, the week in parliament has ended with a revitalised opposition and a wounded LNP government. A government that has for so long seemed untouchable. A government that has now been left battling the perception that it is overseeing a broken health system And a government – now in office for more than two years – finally forced to take responsibility for systems it had promised to repair; seemingly no longer able to legitimately blame the former Labor government for the litany of mistakes that led to the deaths of seven people in the care of Queensland’s health system Another man had taken his own life in the emergency department of the Prince Charles hospital after self-admitting for mental health treatment. It took staff three hours to find him Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The health minister, Tim Nicholls, is a professional, a 20-year veteran, with the bearing of a well-paid barrister, who led the LNP to an election in 2017 But he struggled to cope with the parliamentary barrage In response to a question from Labor’s Joe Kelly, a former nurse, about how many ambulances had been ramped on 3 November, the night a man died while waiting for one in Townsville, Nicholls first criticised the question’s “pettiness” “What next? Are they going to ask me what the level of fuel was in the back of the ambulances?” he responded “There was no ramping overnight at the Townsville University hospital that night,” he finished But that was wrong “I am very pleased to be able to correct the record for the purposes of the house,” he said, two questions later “There were at that time four ambulances, as I understand it, on the ramp waiting to off-load. That was the situation there.” Nicholls threw the blame at the federal government, at the former Labor state government and its “decade of decline”, a phrase repeated endlessly by government MPs, at overwhelmed hospitals full of “forgotten Australians”, a term used to refer to retirees warehoused in public hospitals for lack of a federally funded retirement home to put them in Endlessly, Labor hounded him: would he meet the families of the dead? The answer was not quite no, but never yes either For a government built on a small-target strategy based on responding to the grief of victims of crime – predicated on the fact that any indecisive response to a tragedy would be an inherently unconvincing one – this was a completely different emotional battle The next day, after another bruising question time, he called a press conference Bearing his well-worn years-old folder labelled “LABOR’S HOSPITAL FAILURES”, he insisted that he was taking responsibility – for making sure his subordinates were doing their jobs “I think people would expect that, as the minister, I hold the DG and the commissioner responsible for the services that they deliver, and I seek answers to questions,” he said “So I sought advice from the commissioner about the steps that they were taking, what was being done to address the need, what was the root cause of the problem.” Nicholls said the community could have confidence in the triple-zero system and paramedics, promising to reinvest whatever it was he needed to, on advice from his department “Like all Queenslanders, I do have questions regarding the delivery of services because one death that’s unexpected in the community is one too many,” he said “Every available vehicle is on the road. But the issue is there are simply not enough beds.” After 10 minutes, with many more questions unasked, he abruptly walked off, looking more like a traditional Queensland health minister than any in the LNP cabinet have this term Then Miles stepped up to the microphone. After days of leadership speculation in newspapers – which has been deliberately and mischievously fanned by the government – the former health minister was on much more solid ground “I have never before seen so many preventable deaths of Queenslanders left waiting hours for an ambulance to arrive, only to die before it does,” Miles said “Six, seven, maybe more preventable deaths “It is only getting worse and worse. The worst that it’s ever been.” Miles retains significant goodwill from most Labor MPs, but the polls have become hard for most to ignore. Some think he’s simply failed to land enough punches. Others that he hasn’t thrown nearly enough It remains to be seen whether Miles’s decision to come out swinging was the act of an opposition leader with nothing to lose, deciding to fight at five minutes to midnight in his political career One thing is certain. After two years in which the opposition has rarely felt relevant, this week Queensland politics finally felt like a fair fight

selected_news.quality_narration: Queensland LNP hükümeti, iki yıldan fazla iktidarda olmasına rağmen, sağlık sistemindeki yedi ölüm ve bir intiharı sorumluluk almaya zorlandı. Muhalefet lideri Steven Miles, hastanelerde bekleme süresinin saatlerce uzaması nedeniyle "önlenebilir ölümler" sayısının arttığını belirtti. Miles, LNP'yi eski Labor hükümetini suçlamaktan vazgeçip, kendi sağlık politikalarını düzeltmeye çağırdı.
